text: Hi, I'm Sen, an AI interviewer. This call is transcribed. Ready to begin?
Tell me about a project you led and your role in it.

I led the rebuild of our payments ledger to double-entry event sourcing. I designed the migration with dual writes and a reconciliation job, then cut over service by service. We handled four million transactions a day and I mentored four engineers through it.
How would you design a rate limiter for a public API that serves many customers? Walk me through your approach.

I would use a token bucket per customer key, because it allows short bursts while enforcing a steady average rate. Each request takes a token. I would store the bucket state in Redis and update it atomically with a Lua script so there are no race conditions. I would return 429 with a Retry-After header, and give each customer tier its own limits.
How would this work across multiple servers?

Across servers the shared Redis becomes the source of truth, sharded by customer key with consistent hashing. To cut latency I would let each node keep a small local allowance and sync in batches, accepting slight overshoot in exchange for fewer round trips.
What happens when your shared store is unavailable?

If Redis is down I would fail open for most customers so an outage does not become an API outage, with a coarse local limiter as a safety net so abusive traffic is still capped. For sensitive endpoints like login I would fail closed. I would alert on the fallback path and test it with fault injection.
Thank you. The team will review this and follow up. Goodbye.
